newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bavarian CSU on offensive for strict EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bavarian CSU on offensive for strict EMU.

text.p: Bavaria's Christian Social Union (CSU) party, a core part of the German coalition government, made clear on Wednesday it would tolerate no loosening of any element of Europe's planned currency union.

Asserting itself as Europe's most vocal political force behind a "hard" economic and monetary union (EMU), the party led by German Finance Minister Theo Waigel also insisted that the project should go ahead on time in 1999.
"In practice, it must be assumed any delay in the euro would jeopardise the whole currency union project," CSU deputy chairman and European deputy Ingo Friedrich said in a statement.

"Thus a responsible German policy in this area must be based on a strict insistence both on the criteria and start-date (for EMU)," he added, referring to agreed economic convergence targets and the planned 1999 start-date.

The statement follows reports last week that members of the CSU would push for a delay of EMU following the election of the Socialists in France, whom they fear would seek to loosen the criteria for entry into the currency union.
A CSU spokesman said the statement was issued in the light of the wider discussion over EMU delay and was not directed at its party members in particular.
Earlier, a senior CSU executive issued a direct warning to France's new Socialist government not to tamper with existing agreements guiding currency union.

"The Socialist government in Paris must realise there can be no softening of the Maastricht criteria (for EMU entry) nor any shift away from existing treaty pacts," CSU parliamentary Michael Glos said in the Bayernkurier party newspaper.

Glos said this applied particularly to the so-called stability pact, a Waigel initiative designed to ensure the future stability of the euro by censuring EMU participants whose economies fail to meet agreed performance targets.
The new left-wing French government was elected on promises to reorient the push towards EMU away from its current austerity-based course towards a jobs and economic growth focus.

Earlier this week, Paris caused widespread concern by saying it might not be ready to ratify the stability pact at next week's EU summit in Amsterdam. It has since indicated however that it might yet be able to agree the pact in time.

A further strengthening of the CSU's line is expected when Edmund Stoiber, the CSU-affiliated premier of Bavaria's state government, later on Wednesday delivers a speech on the aims of next week's EU summit in Amsterdam.

Stoiber, believed to harbour ambitions to replace Waigel as the party's next leader, is likely to insist that Waigel continues to trim German deficits to within the precise limits laid out by the Maastricht Treaty on EMU.

With an estimated 10 to 15 billion marks in savings or extra receipts still needing to be found to achieve this, such a move would increase yet further the political pressure already piling up on the beleaguered finance minister.
